pharm: An oral fibric acid derivative (fibrate) used to treat hyperlipidemia; it activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (and to some extent the other PPAR isoforms), increasing lipoprotein lipase activity and fatty-acid oxidation, which lowers serum triglycerides and to a lesser extent LDL cholesterol while raising HDL cholesterol.

Reduce dose / avoid in impairment; contraindicated in severe disease
Limit - can raise triglycerides and add hepatic risk
Lipids, LFTs, renal function/CK, signs of myopathy
summary: Bezafibrate is a fibric acid derivative (fibrate) used to treat hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia, particularly when diet and lifestyle measures are insufficient, and may be used in combination with a statin in selected patients with caution. By activating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-alpha), it enhances lipoprotein lipase activity and hepatic fatty-acid oxidation, lowering triglycerides and VLDL, modestly reducing LDL cholesterol, and raising HDL cholesterol. The usual dose is 200 mg three times daily or a 400 mg modified-release tablet once daily, taken with food. It is largely renally excreted, so dose reduction is needed in renal impairment and it is contraindicated in severe renal or hepatic disease, gallbladder disease, and pregnancy/lactation. Like other fibrates it can cause myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (risk increased with statins and in renal impairment) and may potentiate oral anticoagulants. It is not FDA-approved; dosing and warnings follow the European SmPC and BNF.
indications: Treatment of severe hypertriglyceridemia with or without low HDL cholesterol
Treatment of mixed (combined) hyperlipidemia when a statin is contraindicated or not tolerated, or in addition to a statin with caution
Hyperlipidemia (types IIa, IIb, III, IV, V) inadequately controlled by diet and other appropriate measures

Swallow whole; the modified-release form is generally not used if CrCl is reduced

dosage.d: Reduce dose/frequency per creatinine clearance (e.g., 400 mg once daily or less often)
dosage.t: Once daily or every 1-2 days per CrCl

Swallow modified-release tablets whole; do not crush or chew
Use only as an adjunct to an appropriate lipid-lowering diet and other non-drug measures
Reduce the dose according to renal function and avoid the modified-release form in renal impairment
Assess baseline and periodic lipids, liver function, renal function, and creatine kinase; advise patients to report muscle pain/weakness
moa: Bezafibrate is a fibric acid derivative that acts as an agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-alpha), with some activity at the gamma and delta isoforms. Activation of PPAR-alpha alters transcription of genes controlling lipid metabolism: it increases the expression and activity of lipoprotein lipase and reduces apolipoprotein C-III, accelerating the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (VLDL); it stimulates hepatic fatty-acid uptake and beta-oxidation, lowering hepatic triglyceride and VLDL production; and it increases synthesis of apolipoproteins A-I and A-II, raising HDL cholesterol. The net effect is a marked fall in serum triglycerides, a modest reduction in LDL cholesterol, and an increase in HDL cholesterol.

absolute: Significant hepatic impairment (including primary biliary cholangitis)
Known hypersensitivity to bezafibrate or other fibrates
History of photoallergic or phototoxic reaction to fibrates
relative: Moderate renal impairment (reduce dose; avoid modified-release form)
monitor: Renal function (and creatine kinase if myopathy suspected)
Signs/symptoms of myopathy (muscle pain, tenderness, weakness)

preg: Bezafibrate is contraindicated in pregnancy. It should not be used by pregnant women; effective contraception is advised during treatment in women of childbearing potential.
lact: Bezafibrate is contraindicated during breastfeeding because it is not known whether it is excreted in human milk and because of potential adverse effects on the infant.
renal: Bezafibrate is predominantly excreted by the kidneys, and accumulation increases the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Reduce the dose and frequency in mild-to-moderate renal impairment according to creatinine clearance, avoid the modified-release formulation in renal impairment, and contraindicate use in severe renal impairment and in patients on dialysis.
hepatic: Bezafibrate is contraindicated in significant hepatic impairment, including primary biliary cholangitis. Monitor liver function tests during therapy and discontinue if transaminases rise persistently.

major: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) - markedly increased risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis; combine only with caution and monitoring
Oral anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin) - bezafibrate potentiates anticoagulant effect; reduce anticoagulant dose and monitor INR closely
moderate: Sulfonylureas and insulin - may enhance hypoglycemic effect; monitor blood glucose
Ciclosporin and other nephrotoxic/immunosuppressive agents - increased risk of renal impairment and myopathy
Bile acid sequestrants (e.g., colestyramine) - reduce bezafibrate absorption; separate dosing by at least 2 hours
MAO inhibitors with hepatotoxic potential - avoid concurrent use
minor: Estrogens may raise lipids and partly oppose the effect
interactions.food: Take with or after food to improve tolerance; absorption is adequate with meals.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - it can raise triglycerides and add to hepatic risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Can elevate serum creatinine, transaminases, and creatine kinase; monitor lipid profile, LFTs, renal function, and CK as indicated.

serious: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (especially with statins or in renal impairment)
rare: Severe skin reactions (e.g., erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
emergency: Rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle pain/weakness with dark urine and rising CK)

monitoring: Fasting lipid profile to assess response (and to consider stopping if no adequate effect after a few months)
Renal function (and creatine kinase if muscle symptoms occur)
Symptoms of myopathy (muscle pain, tenderness, weakness)
INR in patients on oral anticoagulants
Blood glucose in patients on antidiabetic therapy
counsel: Take this medicine with or after food, and keep following your low-fat diet and exercise plan
Report any unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness right away, especially with dark urine
Swallow modified-release tablets whole - do not crush or chew them
Tell your doctor if you are on a blood thinner (warfarin) or a statin - your doses and tests may need adjusting
Avoid pregnancy and breastfeeding while taking this medicine, and limit alcohol
Keep your appointments for blood tests to check your cholesterol, liver, and kidneys
pk: Lipid effects develop over days to a few weeks
Elimination half-life ~1-2 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Dosed three times daily or once daily (modified-release)
Store below 25-30 C, protect from light and moisture
pearls: Fibrate / PPAR-alpha agonist - most effective at lowering triglycerides and raising HDL; modest LDL reduction
Largely renally excreted - reduce dose in renal impairment, avoid the modified-release form, and contraindicate in severe renal disease/dialysis (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk)
Combining with a statin substantially raises the risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis - use together only with caution and monitoring
Potentiates oral anticoagulants - reduce warfarin dose and monitor INR
Contraindicated in significant hepatic impairment, gallbladder disease, pregnancy, and lactation
Not FDA-approved - dosing and safety follow the EMA SmPC and BNF
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember with some food. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule - do not take a double dose to make up for it.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Overdose may cause gastrointestinal symptoms and, particularly in renal impairment, an increased risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. Management is supportive with symptomatic treatment, maintenance of renal function and hydration, and monitoring for muscle injury (creatine kinase) and hepatic effects; hemodialysis is not expected to be effective because bezafibrate is highly protein-bound.
